extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law, and church–state relations (general educated public interested in Hobbesian theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Extract and evaluate normative principles and procedural rules about law, conscience, and ecclesiastical power as presented in a classical political-philosophical text (Hobbes). Focus is on doctrines that justify or oppose clerical authority and on rules about sovereignty, obedience, and conquest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of Good and Evil in a Commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: In a Common-wealth the measure [of Good and Evill] is not the appetite of private men, but the Law, which is the Will and Appetite of the State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private judgment of good/evil (measuring by individual passions) is false and pernicious to the public state; subjects ought to regard public law rather than private appetites when judging actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage is not repugnant to Chastity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is vain and false philosophy to say the work of Marriage is repugnant to Chastity or Continence; to call lawful use of wives 'want of Chastity' is mistaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments that forbid clerical marriage are historically contingent (practical for persecuted preachers) or motivated by clerical design to secure worldly power; one should distinguish moral/philosophical grounds from institutional/political motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of calling non-popular governments 'tyranny'
rubrics_metrics.description: From Aristotle's politics many learned to call all commonwealths but the popular 'tyranny'—but the use of such names reflects popular hatred, not objective defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels (tyrant, anarchy, oligarchy) are often rhetorical; one should not equate non-popular rule automatically with unjust tyranny without examining the facts about governance and order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error of 'Not Men, but Law Governs'
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an error to think that in a well-ordered commonwealth not Men should govern, but the Laws; laws without the hands and swords of men cannot in practice hurt or enforce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that laws require enforcement (men and arms); misunderstanding this induces people to oppose governors as 'tyrants' and to endorse rebellion without appreciating that force, not words, upholds law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on Civil Power over Conscience
rubrics_metrics.description: It is erroneous to extend civil law (rule of actions) to the inner thoughts and consciences of men by inquisitions and forcing confession of opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The civil magistrate may require conformity of speech/actions for employment (e.g., a minister must accept to preach certain doctrines to be employed) but cannot legitimately compel persons to accuse themselves of opinions when their actions are not forbidden; forcing inner belief is against the law of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private Interpretation of the Law is Improper
rubrics_metrics.description: A private man, without authority of the commonwealth, to interpret the law by his own spirit is an error; the power of making laws includes the power of explaining them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scriptures and other materials where they are made law become part of civil law through sovereign authority; private reinterpretation or monopolization of preaching where the state leaves it free is an unlawful restriction of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obscure Scholastic Language Conceals Truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The writings of school-divines mostly consist of insignificant trains of strange and barbarous words or words otherwise used than in common Latin, which hide truth and make men think they possess it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test intelligibility by translating into modern tongues; use of obscure terminology is a sign that doctrine might be concealing ignorance or error and discouraging further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject Reliance on Unverified Traditions (Miracles, Apparitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legends of fictitious miracles, apparitions, and unwritten traditions (the 'unwritten Word of God') are unwarranted foundations for doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fathers and early writers are fallible and susceptible to false reports; such testimony should be examined and not accepted as decisive proof of doctrinal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to Suppression of True Philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppression of true philosophy by those lacking lawful authority or competence is an error; punishing or silencing inquiry is wrong when the opinions are not proven contrary to religion or to public peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Truth should be examined by competent judges and, if necessary, refuted by those who claim contrary knowledge; civil law (not ecclesiastical usurpation) should handle disobedience that disturbs public peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cui Bono (Presumption from Benefit)
rubrics_metrics.description: He that receiveth benefit by a fact is presumed to be the author; asking 'Cui bono?' (Who benefits?) is a strong presumption in assigning authorship or motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the benefit test to evaluate who invented or advanced doctrines — doctrines that confer worldly benefits indicate probable authorship by beneficiaries (e.g., papal power).

rubrics_metrics.name: Question Doctrine that Church on Earth is Kingdom of God
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that the present Church militant on earth is the Kingdom of God has been used to claim civil governing rights and to make pastors 'God's public ministers' with power over commonwealths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such doctrines with suspicion because they confer worldly authority and allow ecclesiastical figures (e.g., the Pope) to claim obedience akin to that owed to sovereigns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Papal Infallibility as a Means to Obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that 'the Pope in his public capacity cannot err' functions to secure unquestioning obedience to papal commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the political effect: claimed infallibility reduces resistance and increases papal influence over temporal matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjection of Bishops to the Pope
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching that bishops derive their right from the Pope (not from God or the civil sovereign) creates powerful ecclesiastical figures dependent on a foreign prince, enabling interference and civil conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate episcopal claims of authority by their political consequences and by whether they undermine sovereign jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemptions of Clergy from Civil Law
rubrics_metrics.description: Exempting priests, monks, and friars from civil laws and public charges creates a class protected against penalties and not contributing to public expense, thereby undermining civil authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such exemptions generate a body of subjects more loyal to the Pope than to the civil sovereign and reduce the state's capacity to enforce law and collect revenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titling Priests 'Sacerdotes' and Making the Lord's Supper a Sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Calling priests 'sacerdotes' (sacrificers) and treating the Lord's Supper as a sacrifice endows clergy with symbolic parity to Jewish high priests, implying broad civil and ecclesiastical power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of sacrificial language that conflates spiritual offices with temporal authority; terminology can be used to justify expanded jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Marriage a Sacrament (Clerical Control over Legitimacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching that matrimony is a sacrament gives the clergy authority to judge the lawfulness of marriages and thus to determine legitimacy and succession rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrinal move has clear political effects on inheritance and sovereign succession; its presence signals clerical influence over temporal succession disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of Marriage to Priests as a Political Tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Denying marriage to priests serves to assure papal power over kings (if a king were a priest he could not marry and transmit kingdom), and more broadly to secure clerical leverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess supposed celibacy rules for their institutional benefits to clerical power, not merely on ostensible spiritual grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auricular Confession as Political Intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Auricular confession supplies clergy with privileged knowledge about princes' and great men's designs, thereby strengthening ecclesiastical political leverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat confession practices as potential instruments of surveillance and influence rather than merely private spiritual practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonization and Declaring Martyrs as Means of Social Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Canonizing saints and declaring martyrs induces people to resist civil authorities (even to death) when ecclesiastical powers excommunicate individuals as heretics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize these practices' capacity to provoke civil disobedience and to solidify ecclesiastical authority by sacralizing opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transubstantiation, Penance, and Absolution as Instruments of Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines that ascribe to priests the power of making Christ (transubstantiation) and of ordaining penance and remitting sins create a spiritual dependence that enforces obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such sacramental powers have political consequences: they make subjects reliant on clergy for salvation-related assurances, which can be leveraged to exert temporal control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purgatory, Indulgences, and Justification by External Works as Revenue Sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachings about purgatory, indulgences, and justification by external works function to enrich the clergy materially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate these doctrines for their financial incentives and the way they tie lay practice to clerical revenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daemonology and Exorcism to Maintain Awe
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of daemonology and exorcism keeps people in fear and awe of ecclesiastical power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These practices operate psychologically to maintain clerical prestige and social control; their presence suggests manipulation of fears rather than purely doctrinal concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Scholastic Metaphysics (School-Divinity) to Conceal Error
rubrics_metrics.description: The metaphysics, ethics, and politics of Aristotle and the scholastic distinctions taught in papally regulated universities serve to hide errors and present vanity as gospel truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obscure technical distinctions and learned-sounding jargon can be used institutionally to prevent detection of false doctrines and to perpetuate clerical authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifying Authors of Spiritual Darkness by Benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors of 'spiritual darkness' (doctrines that secure unlawful power) are those who derive manifest profit from them — principally the Pope and Roman clergy, and others who help settle such doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the cui bono rule; also recognize that civil rulers who initially enabled ecclesiastical encroachments are accessories and share responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Dissolution (Reverse Untying of Knots)
rubrics_metrics.description: The resolution of papal authority should proceed by untying the knots in reverse order: dissolve papal power first, then episcopacy, then presbytery — as exemplified by English reforms (Elizabeth, abolition of papal power; later suppression of episcopacy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stepwise, historical approach to dismantling ecclesiastical political authority is recommended rather than abrupt or disorderly measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: No Power Over Conscience Except the Word
rubrics_metrics.description: In a return to primitive Christian independence, there should be no power over men's consciences except the Word itself working faith; individuals may follow Paul, Cephas, or Apollos as they prefer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conscience and belief should be governed by Scripture and personal reason, not by imposed human authority; teachers should not demand obedience that substitutes for personal judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconciliation of Contrary Human Faculties by Education
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrary faculties of the mind (judgment vs. fancy, eloquence vs. solid reasoning, courage vs. timorousness) can be reconciled and ordered through education and discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that conflicting capacities make cohesive civil duty impossible; cultivation and alternating use of faculties allow a single person to perform diverse civil roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Duty to Protect Authority that Protects You in Peace
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man is by nature bound, as much as in him lies, to protect in war the authority by which he is himself protected in time of peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated as a law of nature reinforcing obligation to the commonwealth's authority; it counters claims of private right to destroy the protector on grounds of self-preservation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for When a Subject Becomes Obliged to a Conqueror
rubrics_metrics.description: A man becomes subject to a conqueror at the point when, having liberty to submit to him, he consents (either by express words or other sufficient sign) to be his subject; liberty to submit exists when the means of his life are within enemy guards and garrisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission or composition under conquest is to be understood practically (when survival depends on the enemy's protection) and is not necessarily unlawful assistance to the enemy; timing and consent matter.
